title: Intents API transaction signing
summary: Let an agent sign and submit an on-chain transaction while the private key stays in the vault.

blocks.text: The Intents API lets an agent sign transactions without ever seeing the raw private key. The vault decrypts the key inside the HSM, signs, and broadcasts. The agent only gets back a tx_hash.

items: POST /v1/agents/:id/transactions signs and broadcasts
POST /v1/agents/:id/transactions/sign signs only (BYORPC), returns signed_tx
Unified POST /v1/agents/:id/sign takes intent_type: personal_sign, typed_data, or transaction

blocks.text: The intents_api_enabled flag is two-sided. It grants the transaction endpoints and also blocks direct reads of private_key or ssh_key through the normal secrets endpoint, so the agent can only use keys through the proxy.

steps.text: Get a human API key from the dashboard. Replace with your 1ck_ key from Settings → API Keys.
Create an agent with intents_api_enabled and guardrails. Replace 0xRecipient with a real Ethereum address: use the same address in the transaction to field later.
steps.code:
AGENT_RESPONSE=$(curl -s -X POST "https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "name": "DeFi Bot",
    "intents_api_enabled": true,
    "tx_allowed_chains": ["sepolia", "base"],
    "tx_to_allowlist": ["0xRecipient"],
    "tx_max_value_eth": "0.01",
    "tx_daily_limit_eth": "0.05"
  }')
echo "$AGENT_RESPONSE"

steps.text: Extract the agent id and api_key from the creation response. The agent id is at .agent.id and the api_key is at the top level. The ocv_ key is shown only once: save it.
Provision an HSM-backed Ethereum signing key for the agent (using $AGENT_ID from the previous step). The private key lands in the __agent-keys vault.
Exchange the agent api_key for a JWT (using $AGENT_ID and $AGENT_API_KEY captured earlier).
steps.code:
export AGENT_JWT=$(curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/auth/agent-token \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"agent_id\":\"$AGENT_ID\",\"api_key\":\"$AGENT_API_KEY\"}" | jq -r .access_token)

steps.text: Submit a transaction on Sepolia with simulate_first so a revert returns 422 and nothing is signed. Replace 0xRecipient with a real Ethereum address. Use the same address in both tx_to_allowlist and the transaction to field.

blocks.text: Signing keys provisioned as 'ethereum' work on Sepolia and other EVM chains allowed by your guardrails.
Fund the returned address with Sepolia ETH from a faucet (e.g. sepoliafaucet.com) before submitting a real transaction.
Want to sign but broadcast yourself? Call /transactions/sign with the same body. You get signed_tx and tx_hash back, and all guardrails still apply.
You now have an agent that submits a simulated, guardrailed transaction with the signing key locked inside the vault.

quiz.question: What does intents_api_enabled: true do besides granting the transaction endpoints?
options: It exports the private key to the agent
It blocks the agent from reading private_key or ssh_key via the secrets endpoint
It rotates the signing key nightly
quiz.explanation: The flag is two-sided: it grants transaction endpoints and blocks direct signing-key reads so keys are only usable through the proxy.

quiz.question: What happens when simulate_first: true and the simulation reverts?
options: The API returns 422 and does not sign or broadcast
quiz.explanation: On a reverted simulation the API returns 422 and never signs or broadcasts.

quiz.question: Which endpoint signs a transaction without broadcasting it?
quiz.explanation: The /transactions/sign endpoint returns signed_tx for you to broadcast yourself, with guardrails still enforced.

concepts.note: signing versus encryption, and blind signing

title: Treasury wallets and smart accounts
summary: Create human-owned multi-chain treasury wallets and drive a Safe multisig with proposals.

blocks.text: Treasury wallets are native HSM-backed wallets for human users across six chains. Keys are generated server-side, stored in a per-org __treasury-keys vault, and never leave the enclave unless you export them.

Treasury wallets require a Pro or higher plan and enforce require_human. Agents calling any treasury wallet endpoint get a 403. Direct API reads of __treasury-keys also return 403; use the export endpoint instead.

items: Six chains: Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana, XRP, Cardano, Tron
Custody is XOR 2-of-2 on Pro and Team, Shamir 2-of-3 on Business and Enterprise
Safe multisig proposals collect signatures and auto-execute at threshold
Agent delegation modes: Owner (agent EOA is a Safe signer) or Delegated (agent signs with the treasury key via Intents API)

steps.text: Use a human API key. Free tier gets a 403 here. Replace with your 1ck_ key from Settings → API Keys.
Generate treasury wallets. Omit chains to create all six.
Create a treasury bound to a Safe address so you can manage signers and proposals. Use the address of an existing deployed Safe multisig.
Export the treasury ID from the creation response.

Create a multisig proposal against that treasury. Build the Safe transaction off-chain using the Safe SDK (@safe-global/protocol-kit) or the Safe Transaction Service API. Compute the EIP-712 safe_tx_hash and read the current Safe nonce from the Safe service.
Export the proposal ID from the creation response.

Sign the proposal. When approve signatures reach the Safe threshold, the proposal auto-executes and broadcasts. signer_address must be a Safe owner. signature is the EIP-712 approval signature for the safe_tx_hash, produced by that owner's key.
Poll GET /v1/treasury/$TREASURY_ID/proposals/$PID until status is 'executed'.

blocks.text: Treasury wallet generation creates org-held HSM keys. Creating a treasury links an existing Safe for multisig proposals. These are related but distinct concepts.
In Delegated mode the agent submits transactions through the Intents API with treasury_id and mode: treasury. The handler applies the strictest of the agent-level and delegation-level guardrails.
You now have a treasury wallet and a Safe proposal that collects signatures and executes on its own once threshold is met.

quiz.question: Why does an agent get a 403 when calling a treasury wallet endpoint?
options: The agent has no signing key
quiz.explanation: All treasury wallet endpoints enforce require_human, so agents receive a 403.

quiz.question: In Delegated mode, where does the treasury private key live when an agent signs?
options: It is copied to the agent
It stays in __treasury-keys and signs via the Intents API
It is returned in the response
It moves to the Safe contract
quiz.explanation: Delegated mode signs with the treasury key through the Intents API; the key never leaves __treasury-keys.

quiz.question: What triggers a Safe proposal to execute automatically?
options: Approve signatures reaching the Safe threshold
quiz.explanation: When approve signatures reach the Safe threshold, the proposal auto-executes and broadcasts.

title: x402 micropayments for overages
summary: Handle an HTTP 402 from the API and retry with an on-chain payment proof.

blocks.text: When your org is over its monthly request quota and the overage method is x402, payable endpoints return 402 Payment Required. You pay on Base with USDC and retry with an X-PAYMENT header.

items: 402 body is spec-compliant with an accepts[] array
accepts[] uses scheme exact, network eip155:8453, asset USDC on Base
Amounts are atomic units (USDC has 6 decimals, so 1500 is 0.0015 USDC)
1Claw settles through the Coinbase CDP facilitator on Base (chain 8453)

blocks.text: New orgs default to credits for overages. Switch to x402 explicitly before you rely on per-request on-chain payment.

steps.text: Set your credentials. Replace with your 1ck_ key from Settings → API Keys. Use your vault UUID from 1claw vault list or Foundations.
Switch the org overage method to x402.
Hit a payable endpoint. When over quota you get a 402 with accepts[].
Read the 402 accepts[] entry: scheme, network, maxAmountRequired, payTo, and asset.
Clone the x402 example from github.com/1clawAI/1claw-examples (or see the retry pattern below). Generate an EOA key, fund it with USDC on Base, and let an x402 client sign the payment and retry.
steps.code:
git clone https://github.com/1clawAI/1claw-examples.git
cd 1claw-examples/x402-payments
npm install && cp .env.example .env
# set X402_PRIVATE_KEY, TOKEN, VAULT_ID
npm start

steps.text: Alternatively, retry the request inline with an X-PAYMENT header containing the payment proof from your x402 client.

blocks.text: A 402 response requires BOTH conditions: (1) overage_method set to x402, and (2) your monthly quota is exhausted. The example below is illustrative; you will only see 402 after exceeding your plan's quota.
Run npm run probe with no payment key to confirm the 402 behavior before you fund a wallet. It only sends GET requests and prints status codes.
You can now take a 402, sign a USDC payment on Base, and retry the same request with X-PAYMENT to get a 200.

quiz.question: Which network and asset do 1Claw x402 payments use?
quiz.explanation: The accepts[] entry uses network eip155:8453 with USDC on Base, settled via the Coinbase CDP facilitator.

quiz.question: The 402 shows maxAmountRequired: 1500 for USDC. What is that?
quiz.explanation: Amounts are atomic units and USDC has 6 decimals, so 1500 is 0.0015 USDC.

quiz.question: After the API returns 402, how does the client complete the request?
options: It waits for the quota to reset
It signs the payment and retries with an X-PAYMENT header
quiz.explanation: An x402 client pays the required amount on-chain and retries with the X-PAYMENT header.

title: Embedded wallets and wallet-react
summary: Give users an email-login wallet and render it with the wallet-react widget.

blocks.text: Embedded wallets give users a wallet from just an email address. No extensions, no seed phrases. You provision them with a platform app key and email OTP login.
You need a Pro or higher plan and a platform app plt_ key created in the dashboard at the Platform page.

steps.text: Install both SDKs.
Create a platform app from the dashboard or via API (see Compliance & Operations), then note its slug; that is what both the SDK and the widget identify the app by.
Create the client with your platform app key. Replace with your platform app key from the dashboard. This key is shown only once at app creation.
steps.code:
import { createClient } from "@1claw/sdk";
const client = createClient({ baseUrl: "https://api.1claw.co", apiKey: "plt_..." });

steps.text: Send a login code to the user's email.
Verify the 6-digit code and auto-provision an Ethereum wallet. Every SDK call resolves to { data, error, meta }, so read the fields off data.
Set a spend policy so users cannot move more than you allow.

Drop the widget into your app. appId is the platform app slug and is required. features is an object of toggles, not an array, and socialProviders accepts google, apple, or discord: email login goes through the OTP flow above.

blocks.text: Steps 3-5 show the SDK auth flow (useful for backend or headless apps). Step 7 shows the React widget, which handles auth standalone via social providers. Choose the path that fits your use case.
You can override the app-wide spend policy per user with client.platform.setUserSpendPolicy(connectionId, {...}).
You now render a working embedded wallet widget backed by email OTP login and a spend policy.

OneclawEmbeddedWallet is standalone and needs no provider. Reach for OneclawWalletProvider plus the useOneclawWallet hook only when you are building custom wallet UI; it takes apiKey and appId and gives you wallets, balances, send, swap and loginWithEmailOtp to wire up yourself.

quiz.question: What do you need before creating embedded wallets?
options: A Free plan and a 1ck_ key
A Pro+ plan and a platform app plt_ key
quiz.explanation: Embedded wallets require a Pro or higher plan plus a platform app plt_ key.

quiz.question: How does a user log in to get a wallet?
options: Email OTP with sendEmailOtp and verifyEmailOtp
quiz.explanation: You send a code with sendEmailOtp and confirm it with verifyEmailOtp, which returns the wallet_address.

quiz.question: Which two components does wallet-react provide for the widget?
quiz.explanation: OneclawWalletProvider wraps the OneclawEmbeddedWallet component.

title: Guardrail governance and graduated HITL
summary: Measure a guardrail in shadow mode before enforcing it, and route risky transactions to a human instead of denying them outright.

blocks.text: Hard guardrails answer yes or no. Real operations need a middle setting: route this to a human. Graduated HITL (v0.54-0.55) adds approval policies that return 202 awaiting_approval instead of a refusal.

items: tx_approval_policy: matching transactions wait for a human decision.
typed_data_policy: escalates EIP-712 signing.
simulation_failure_policy: escalates when a simulation fails rather than blindly proceeding.
raw_signing_policy: escalates or denies raw digest signing, which bypasses other guardrails.

blocks.text: Separately, guardrail governance (v0.56) lets you measure a rule before it ever blocks anything. Set enforcement to log and the rule runs in shadow mode: it records what it would have denied, and denies nothing.

steps.text: Put a new rule in shadow mode. It will record decisions without affecting traffic.
After it has seen real traffic, read the shadow report to find out what it would have blocked.
Replay the rule against recent transactions as a dry run, before you commit to it.
steps.code:
curl -s -X POST https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AGENT_ID/guardrails/replay \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN"
# or: 1claw guardrails replay

steps.text: Happy with it? Flip enforcement to enforce.
Add an approval policy so large transfers reach a human rather than failing.

blocks.text: Widening a guardrail does not take effect immediately. Since v0.56.2 a widening edit queues behind a policy_change approval with step-up re-auth, and the PATCH returns 202 with a pending_approval_id. Narrowing edits apply straight away.
Audit the shadow decisions with the guardrail_shadow.would_deny event, and review history through GET /v1/org/guardrail-revisions.

quiz.question: What does enforcement "log" do?
options: Runs the rule in shadow mode, recording what it would deny without denying it
Logs every request to the audit trail
quiz.explanation: Shadow mode measures a rule against real traffic before it can break anything, and the shadow report tells you what would have been blocked.

quiz.question: You widen an agent's guardrail with a PATCH and get back a 202 with a pending_approval_id. Why?
options: Widening edits queue behind a policy_change approval with step-up re-auth
The API is rate limiting you
quiz.explanation: Since v0.56.2 widening access is itself a privileged change: it waits for an approval. Narrowing edits still apply immediately, because they only reduce access.

quiz.question: How does tx_approval_policy differ from a hard spending cap?
options: A matching transaction returns 202 awaiting_approval instead of being refused
It applies only to non-EVM chains
quiz.explanation: A hard cap refuses. An approval policy routes the transaction to a human, so legitimate large transfers can proceed with oversight rather than simply failing.

title: Payment cards over x402
summary: Have an agent order a prepaid card, paid with an on-chain x402 payment, without ever seeing the card number.

blocks.text: An agent can order prepaid and gift cards through 1Claw and never see the PAN or CVV. The purchase is paid with an outbound x402 payment that the Vault constructs and signs using the agent's own Ethereum signing key, which must hold USDC on Base.
PCI posture matters here. For Laso cards only the card_id and an encrypted refresh token are stored; the PAN and CVV are fetched just-in-time at reveal and never persisted.

items: cards_enabled: the master switch.
card_max_order_usd and card_daily_limit_usd: enforced atomically over a rolling 24-hour window.
card_payto_allowlist: which x402 recipients are acceptable.
card_require_approval: defaults to true, so orders wait for a human.

steps.text: Set the ordering guardrails on the agent. These bound the purchase, not how the card is later spent.
steps.code:
curl -s -X PATCH https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AGENT_ID \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "cards_enabled": true,
    "card_max_order_usd": 25,
    "card_daily_limit_usd": 25,
    "card_require_approval": true
  }'

steps.text: As the agent, order a card. Idempotency-Key is required.
Because approval is required you get a 202 with status awaiting_approval, and no payment has been made yet.
A human approves: in the dashboard, the mobile app, or by one-click email link. Only then does the x402 payment run.
Check status. The card monitor polls the provider and fills in last4, expiry, and balance.
steps.code:
1claw card list
1claw card get <card-id>   # always masked to last4

blocks.text: Before signing the EIP-3009 authorization the Vault validates the 402 challenge: payTo must be allowlisted, the network must be Base (eip155:8453), the amount must match, and the asset must equal the pinned Base USDC contract. That validation is the security boundary.

Revealing a card is human-only by default. Agents get a 403 unless a human enabled a per-card reveal_policy. Reveal is deliberately absent from the MCP tool set, so a PAN can never land in a model's context window.

quiz.question: With card_require_approval true, when does the x402 payment actually happen?
options: Only after a human approves the pending approval
Immediately, and it is refunded if rejected
When the card monitor next runs
At the end of the billing period
quiz.explanation: The order returns 202 awaiting_approval and creates a card row in that state. No payment is made until a human approves: rejecting simply marks the card rejected.

quiz.question: Why is the reveal operation deliberately missing from the MCP tool set?
options: So a card number can never be written into a model's context window
Because MCP does not support it technically
quiz.explanation: order_card, list_cards and get_card_status are exposed, but reveal is omitted on purpose to keep PANs out of agent context. Humans reveal through re-authenticated paths.

quiz.question: What does the Vault validate before signing the x402 payment authorization?
options: payTo allowlist, Base network, exact amount, and the pinned USDC contract
Only that the agent has cards_enabled
quiz.explanation: That four-part check on the 402 challenge is the payment security boundary, and it is why a malicious challenge cannot redirect funds elsewhere.

concepts.note: bounding what an agent may spend
why reveal is absent from MCP

title: Portfolio and treasury operations
summary: Read balances across every wallet type from one endpoint, then send, swap, and import keys safely.

blocks.text: An org accumulates wallets in three different shapes: treasury wallets, agent signing keys, and imported smart accounts. The Portfolio API aggregates all of them behind a single call.

steps.text: Get the whole portfolio, with token balances and USD estimates.
Generate native treasury wallets. Six chains are supported: Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana, XRP, Cardano, Tron.
Send from a treasury wallet. Non-EVM chains take chain-specific fields: a destination_tag for XRP, a fee rate for Bitcoin, a memo for Solana.
Send gaslessly by wrapping it as an ERC-4337 UserOperation with paymaster sponsorship.
Bring your own key. Import is human-only and requires password re-auth.

blocks.text: Treasury private keys live in a per-org __treasury-keys vault with MPC custody set automatically by tier: XOR 2-of-2 on Pro and Team, Shamir 2-of-3 across multiple HSMs on Business and Enterprise.

Direct API reads of __treasury-keys and __agent-keys are blocked with a 403. Private keys only ever come out through the designated export endpoints, which require password re-authentication and are audit-logged.
Treasury wallets are human-only: agents get a 403. Swap remains EVM-only, while send now covers all six chains.

quiz.question: What does GET /v1/portfolio aggregate?
options: Treasury wallets, agent signing keys, and smart accounts
Only wallets with a non-zero balance
quiz.explanation: It is a unified aggregator across all three wallet types, with optional token balances and USD estimates.

quiz.question: Why does reading __treasury-keys directly return 403?
options: Private keys may only leave through the audited export endpoints
The vault does not exist yet
It requires a Business tier plan
quiz.explanation: Blocking direct reads means there is exactly one path to a private key: the export endpoint, which demands password re-auth and writes an audit record.

quiz.question: Which MPC custody mode applies to a Business-tier org's treasury keys?
quiz.explanation: Custody is set automatically by tier: XOR 2-of-2 for Pro and Team, Shamir 2-of-3 multi-HSM for Business and Enterprise.

title: Bankr dynamic key vending
summary: Lease short-lived partner API keys instead of storing a static one, and keep the key out of agent output entirely.

blocks.text: Some partner credentials should never sit in a vault as a static secret. Bankr key vending is a secret engine: you store one partner key server-side, and 1Claw mints scoped, TTL-bound user keys on demand.

items: The partner key (bk_ptr_) is held server-side as BANKR_PARTNER_KEY.
The Vault issues short-lived bk_usr_ keys scoped to a single agent.
Recommended TTL is 5-15 minutes; the agent default is 15 minutes and the hard maximum is 24 hours.
This is preferred over storing a Bankr credential with put_secret.

blocks.text: Deny-by-default: an agent needs an explicit policy on agents/{id}/bankr/* inside the __agent-keys vault before it can lease anything.

steps.text: Grant the agent leasing rights with a policy on its Bankr path.
Lease a key with a short TTL.
Note what comes back to an agent caller: metadata, but no api_key field.
List and revoke active leases.

blocks.text: Agent lease responses omit api_key on purpose, and the MCP lease_bankr_key tool never returns the key in its output. Shroud resolves the real key at request time, so it never enters the model's context.

The pattern generalises: when a credential can be minted on demand, leasing beats storing. There is nothing long-lived to leak, and expiry is the default rather than something you have to remember to do.

quiz.question: Why does an agent's Bankr lease response omit the api_key field?
options: So the key never enters the agent's context: Shroud resolves it at request time
Because the key is not generated yet
quiz.explanation: The lease gives the agent metadata only. Shroud resolves the actual key when the request is made, so the credential never reaches the model's context window.

quiz.question: What must exist before an agent can lease a Bankr key?
options: A policy on agents/{id}/bankr/* in the __agent-keys vault
quiz.explanation: Bankr vending is deny-by-default. Without an explicit policy on that path the lease is refused.

quiz.question: What is the recommended TTL for a leased Bankr key?
quiz.explanation: 5-15 minutes is recommended; the agent default is 15 minutes and 24 hours is the hard maximum, not a target.

concepts.note: leasing beats storing when a credential can be minted

title: Safe agent accounts
summary: Give an agent a counterfactual Gnosis Safe instead of a bare EOA, and plan the migration off the EOA.

blocks.text: An agent's default identity on an EVM chain is an externally owned account: one key, one signature, no policy on-chain. Safe agent accounts (v0.56.2) let an agent operate through a Gnosis Safe instead, so guardrails can eventually be enforced by the chain rather than only by the Vault.
Provisioning is counterfactual: the Safe address is derived and usable before any deployment transaction is sent, so you can fund and reference it without paying to deploy first.

steps.text: List the accounts an agent currently has, per chain.
steps.code:
curl -s https://api.1claw.co/v1/agents/$AGENT_ID/accounts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ONECLAW_TOKEN"
# or: 1claw agent accounts list $AGENT_ID

steps.text: Provision a counterfactual Safe account for the agent.
Inspect the pinned module registry for the chain: Safe v1.4.1 plus Zodiac. This endpoint is public.
Migrate the agent from its EOA to the Safe.
Once nothing depends on the old EOA, deprecate it so it can no longer be used.

blocks.text: This is a foundation, not a finished feature. The on-chain deploy, cosign, passkey, timelock, and ERC-4337 endpoints deliberately return 501 pending a Guard audit. Provisioning, migration, and the registry work today.
The dashboard has a guided migration wizard at /agents/[agentId]/migrate-safe, and org-wide allowance sync runs through POST /v1/org/safe/sync-allowances.

quiz.question: What does counterfactual provisioning mean here?
options: The Safe address is derived and usable before any deployment transaction is sent
The Safe is deployed immediately on creation
The Safe exists only in the database
quiz.explanation: The address is computed deterministically up front, so you can fund and reference the account without paying deployment gas until it is actually needed.

quiz.question: Why do several Safe endpoints currently return 501?
options: On-chain deploy, cosign, passkey, timelock and 4337 are pending a Guard audit
quiz.explanation: The provisioning and migration foundation ships now; the on-chain execution paths are held back behind 501 until the Guard audit completes.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of a Safe over a bare EOA for an agent?
options: Guardrails can eventually be enforced on-chain rather than only by the Vault
It removes the need for signing keys
quiz.explanation: An EOA is one key with no on-chain policy. A Safe with modules can enforce constraints at the chain level, so a compromised Vault path is not automatically a compromised wallet.

concepts.note: why one key with no on-chain policy is fragile
